job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section read. I've flagged everything that looks exploitable, unclear, or legally fragile; the biggest problems are flagged in a short note at the end.

## Sec. 2(1) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel tonnage threshold invites fleet-splitting.** Because the 10,000-ton limit applies "by a single vessel," an operator can run any number of vessels each recovering 9,999 tons and never trigger the prohibition. The threshold should aggregate across all vessels under common ownership, control, contract, or license area, or be dropped in favor of a purpose-based definition.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "Per year" is undefined.** It is unclear whether this means calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12 months, which lets an operator time recovery across a year boundary (e.g., 9,000 tons in December and 9,000 in January) to stay under the cap in any one period.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Tonnage basis is unspecified (wet vs. dry).** Nodules as recovered carry substantial water weight, and nothing says whether the 10,000 tons is measured as recovered, dried, or processed. An operator will argue for whichever basis keeps it under the line, and NOAA will have nothing to point to.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "Recovery" is undefined and too narrow.** The definition reaches only physically lifting minerals; it says nothing about collecting on the seabed and transferring at sea to a second vessel, seabed-crawler or platform-based systems that are not "vessels," or the processing, transshipment, import, or sale of the minerals. Each of those is a path to keep the enterprise running.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "Other mineral resources" is both over- and under-inclusive.** Read literally, it sweeps in deepwater oil and gas (routinely called "mineral resources" in OCSLA) and sand/aggregate dredging below 200 m, which opponents will use at markup to brand the bill as an offshore energy ban. At the same time it does not expressly name seafloor massive sulfides or cobalt-rich crusts, leaving room to argue those are not "recovery from the seabed" because they are embedded in it.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "The Secretary" is never defined.** No section identifies which Secretary (Commerce, State, Interior) holds this authority, so the catch-all is unusable on its face.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — Open-ended discretionary catch-all with no standard or procedure.** The "comparable risk" determination has no criteria, no rulemaking or notice requirement, no deadline, and no judicial-review provision, so a hostile administration can simply never make one. Worse, because Sec. 5(b) attaches a 10-year felony to this definition, the provision is exposed to void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges that could pull the whole definition down.

## Sec. 2(2) — Definition of "U.S. person"

8. **Sec. 2(2) — Definition omits most business entities.** It covers only "a corporation organized under the laws of a State," leaving out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and entities organized under the laws of D.C., territories, tribes, or federal charter. A mining company can convert to an LLC and exit the prohibition.

9. **Sec. 2(2) — No coverage of foreign subsidiaries or controlled entities.** A U.S. corporation can conduct all mining through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary (the dominant industry model already uses Canadian, Belgian, and Pacific-island entities), and nothing reaches entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons. The definition needs an "owned or controlled by" clause and should cover U.S. nationals, permanent residents, and U.S.-flagged vessels.

## Sec. 3 — Prohibition

10. **Sec. 3(a) — "Any person in the United States" has no reach where mining happens.** Mining occurs at sea, so a foreign company's U.S. office that merely directs, finances, or markets the operation can argue it never "engaged in" mining while "in the United States." The prohibition effectively collapses to U.S. persons only.

11. **Sec. 3(a) — "Engage in" does not reach the supply chain.** There is no prohibition on financing, insuring, chartering, contracting for, providing port or vessel services to, importing, or purchasing the products of commercial deep seabed mining, and no aiding-and-abetting or anti-circumvention clause. Foreign operators keep full access to U.S. capital, ports, and markets.

12. **Sec. 3(a) — Prohibition does not bind the federal government.** "Person" ordinarily excludes federal agencies, so nothing here stops NOAA from issuing permits under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA), Interior from leasing under OCSLA, or DoD from purchasing or stockpiling seabed minerals. The bill never amends or references DSHMRA or OCSLA, setting up a direct conflict with existing permitting statutes that the 2025 executive order directed agencies to accelerate.

13. **Sec. 3(b) — "Exploration license" converts into a perpetual commercial-mining permit.** The term is undefined (DSHMRA licenses? ISA contracts via sponsoring states? any foreign license?), and exploration licenses by their nature do not authorize commercial recovery, yet the exemption would let any holder of one mine commercially forever. This is the single largest loophole in the bill.

14. **Sec. 3(b) — Grandfather date triggers a license rush.** Tying the exemption to licenses "issued before the date of enactment" creates an incentive for NOAA and friendly foreign governments to issue as many licenses as possible between now and signature. At minimum the cutoff should be moved back to the introduction date and the exemption limited in scope and duration.

15. **Sec. 3(c) — "Environmental assessment" exemption has no boundaries.** The term is undefined, there is no tonnage cap, no requirement of a bona fide scientific purpose, no approval, oversight, or reporting, and nothing stops the minerals collected from being sold. Every "pilot" or "test mining" operation will be characterized as assessment.

## Sec. 4 — Registry

16. **Sec. 4 — No penalty for failing to register or report.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so the registry and reporting duties are unenforceable, and there is no express false-statement penalty for the self-certified reports.

17. **Sec. 4 — No jurisdictional nexus or definition of "operator."** The section purports to apply to every covered vessel on earth with no connection to U.S. persons, flag, or ports, which is unenforceable against foreign vessels and may draw a challenge, while "operator" (owner? charterer? manager?) is undefined.

18. **Sec. 2(3)/Sec. 4 — 5,000 GT threshold and "equipped for" are easy to game.** Smaller vessels, barges, and platforms escape the registry entirely, and a vessel can be reconfigured or its equipment staged separately so that it is not "equipped for" recovery at the time of inquiry.

19. **Sec. 4(b) — Reports are self-certified with no verification, inspection, or publication.** There is no NOAA or Coast Guard inspection, boarding, audit, or data-request authority, no deadline for registration, and no public access to the registry, so the only data for enforcing the tonnage threshold is whatever the regulated party chooses to report.

## Sec. 5 — Penalties

20. **Sec. 5(a) — Penalty date conflicts with Sec. 8 effective date.** Civil penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. A defendant will argue either that no penalty can attach in the gap (likely correct) or that the clause is unconstitutionally retroactive; either way it is a drafting error.

21. **Sec. 5(a) — Per-day penalty does not fit an annual-tonnage violation.** Under Sec. 2(1)(A) the violation occurs when a vessel crosses 10,000 tons in a year, so an operator can argue the violation "occurs" on one day only, capping exposure at $1 million for an entire year of mining.

22. **Sec. 5(a) — No enforcement mechanism.** The bill names no agency to assess penalties, no procedure, no injunctive relief, no forfeiture of vessels or minerals, no Coast Guard enforcement authority, and no citizen-suit provision. "Not more than $1,000,000" also sets no floor, so penalties can be nominal.

23. **Sec. 5(b) — "Willfully" plus a vague definition makes criminal enforcement unlikely.** Combined with the undefined "Secretary" and the standardless 2(1)(B) catch-all, the willfulness requirement and vagueness exposure mean prosecutors will rarely bring the felony count.

24. **Sec. 5 — No individual or officer liability.** Penalties run only against "any person who violates," with no provision reaching corporate officers, directors, or beneficial owners who direct a violation through a thinly capitalized entity.

## Sec. 6 — International agreement

25. **Sec. 6 — Purely hortatory and ambiguous deadline.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude anything, has no reporting requirement, and the 18-month clause is ambiguous as to whether negotiations must begin or conclude by then. It also ignores the U.S. position outside UNCLOS and the International Seabed Authority, which will be raised at markup.

## Sec. 7 — Duration

26. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — Internal contradiction.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues until Congress affirmatively finds mining is safe, while (b) ends the entire Act automatically after 10 years. The sunset controls as the more specific provision, which guts (a) and tells investors exactly when to resume.

27. **Sec. 7(b) — Sunset also kills the registry and penalties.** "This Act shall cease to have effect" terminates Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 along with the prohibition, erasing even the transparency baseline.

28. **Sec. 7(a) — No one is required to commission or fund the National Academies report, and "serious harm" is undefined.** Opponents will characterize the off-ramp as illusory, and the lack of any standard invites a future Congress to accept a thin report.

## Sec. 8 and general drafting

29. **Sec. 8 — 180-day delay with no interim restraint.** Operators can mine freely for six months after enactment, and nothing prohibits agencies from issuing new authorizations during that window.

30. **General — Key terms undefined.** "Secretary," "recovery," "operator," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "year," and "seabed" (does it include subsoil?) are all undefined, each of which becomes a litigation point.

31. **General — No rulemaking authority, no severability clause, and no savings clause.** Without rulemaking authority NOAA cannot fill the gaps above, and without severability a successful vagueness challenge to Sec. 2(1)(B) or Sec. 5(b) risks the entire Act.

---

**Priority fixes if you can only get a few into the manager's package:** (a) rewrite Sec. 3(b) so exploration licenses do not authorize commercial recovery; (b) close the "U.S. person" definition to include LLCs and controlled foreign subsidiaries; (c) aggregate the tonnage threshold across fleets or replace it with a purpose-based definition; (d) define "Secretary" and add standards to 2(1)(B); (e) strike or reconcile the Sec. 7(b) sunset; (f) fix the Sec. 5(a)/Sec. 8 date conflict and add penalties for Sec. 4 violations. Happy to draft amendment language for any of these.
